claims.claim: Respirations are the breaths a person takes per minute; the respiratory rate is the measure of breathing.

The adult resting reference range for respirations is about 12 to 20 breaths per minute: OpenStax lists 12 to 20 and MedlinePlus lists 12 to 18, so the lesson presents the range with the honest caveat that references differ slightly at the upper edge.

Normal respiratory rate varies with age: infants breathe 30 to 60 times per minute, toddlers 20 to 30, school-age children 14 to 22, and rates settle toward the adult range in late childhood or early adolescence.
Each breath has two named parts: inhalation (breathing in) and exhalation/expiration (breathing out); the chest rises and falls with each cycle, and each rise-and-fall pair counts as one breath.
Respirations are assessed by rate (breaths per minute), depth (shallow or deep), and pattern/rhythm (regular or irregular), and unlabored breathing is quietly audible at most.
Breathing changes with activity and emotion: mild changes can come from something as simple as hard exercise, and anxiety or fear can speed the rate up (tachypnea).
Illness and pain change breathing: pain can produce shallow breathing, and slow or fast breathing can be a sign of a serious breathing problem.

Respirations are counted without the patient's awareness — the nurse keeps fingers on the pulse site and watches the chest rise and fall — because a patient who knows the count is happening may unknowingly alter the breathing pattern; breathing is partly voluntary.
A resting adult rate above about 20 breaths per minute is tachypnea and below about 12 is bradypnea, by the OpenStax reference.
Respirations are the quiet vital sign: unlike temperature, pulse, or blood pressure, they require only observation, which makes them easy to overlook and worth taking deliberately.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Upper edge of the adult resting respiratory rate range
positions: OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills (section 15.6): adult range 12 to 20 breaths per minute
MedlinePlus (NLM) Vital signs encyclopedia article: breathing 12 to 18 breaths per minute
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the reference as 'about 12 to 20 breaths per minute' with OpenStax attributed, and the honest-caveat paragraph names MedlinePlus's 12 to 18 so readers see that references vary slightly at the edge. The range is framed as a reference for resting adults, not a rule, and age- and activity-related variation is stated explicitly. No single number is presented as universal.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claim that respirations is 'a foundational concept' with no clinical content — unsupported boilerplate, replaced entirely.

The generated draft's toolbox-drawer analogy ('Think of respirations as a label on a toolbox drawer') — generic boilerplate with no source support, replaced with source-verified clinical content and an original analogy.

The generated draft's vocabulary definitions ('A foundational Nursing & Allied Health Foundations concept covered in this lesson') — circular and content-free, replaced with concrete, source-supported definitions.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with source-verified content: the working definition (breaths per minute), the attributed adult resting range of about 12-20 with MedlinePlus's 12-18 named, age variation, inhalation/exhalation naming, rate/depth/pattern, the exercise-emotion-illness-pain changers, and the quiet-counting practice with its rationale.

No specific counting duration (such as 'a full minute') is asserted, because none of the cited sources states one; the lesson describes the practice as watching the chest rise and fall while counting, and the worked example counts over the observation period without inventing a duration.

Oxygen-saturation and blood-pressure content that appears on the OpenStax 15.6 page was left out of scope per the sibling-topic boundary (oxygen-saturation and blood-pressure topics own those subjects).
